research.topic: What a rubric actually does in an eval — it converts a vague quality judgement into a fixed, ordered list of checks that any grader (human or model) applies the same way to every output
research.slo: The learner can take a vague quality complaint about a model output and rewrite it as a rubric of 3-5 independently checkable criteria, each with an explicit pass condition, so that two different graders scoring the same output land on the same score.
research.audience: L&D and product people at Taleemabad building AI features who already know what an eval is and that outputs need to be graded (evals-01 through evals-04), but who so far have graded by reading an output and saying 'yeah, that's good' — no formal training in measurement or rubric design.
key_points: A rubric is not a scoring form for the output — it is a specification of the judgement itself: it fixes WHAT is being looked for before anyone looks

The two topics tangled in 'rubrics' are (a) what a rubric does and (b) how to write good criteria wording. This video covers (a) only — the SLO needs the function, not the craft; criteria wording is the next video
A criterion must be independently checkable: one grader reading only that line, without asking anyone, can say pass or fail
Vague words ('clear', 'good', 'engaging') hide a judgement that lives only in one person's head, so scores move when the person moves — the same output scores differently on Tuesday than Monday
A rubric makes disagreement visible and useful: two graders now disagree about ONE named criterion instead of about a number, and that disagreement is a fixable bug in the rubric
The score is a by-product; the real output of a rubric is that everyone is grading the same thing
research.ali_scenario: Ali is grading AI-generated Grade 4 Urdu reading-comprehension questions for Taleemabad. He has 40 generated questions in a spreadsheet and one column headed 'Quality (1-5)'. He grades all 40 in an afternoon. Then he hands the same 40 to his teammate to double-check, and the two score sheets come back different on 17 of the 40 rows — including question #12, which Ali gave a 4 and his teammate gave a 2.
research.friction: Ali cannot defend a single number. Sitting with question #12 open — a question asking a 9-year-old to 'analyse the author's tone' — he says '4, it reads well.' His teammate says '2, a Grade 4 child cannot answer that.' They are both right, because they were never grading the same thing: Ali was scoring fluency of the Urdu, his teammate was scoring age-appropriateness. Nothing in the spreadsheet said which one 'Quality' meant. Worse, when Ali re-grades ten rows the next morning to settle it, he changes three of his own scores. The 40 numbers are unusable — he cannot tell the model team what to fix, because 'raise the average from 3.1 to 4' names no defect.
research.fix: Ali stops scoring and instead writes down, before looking at any question, the four things he was actually checking all along, one line each, each answerable yes/no by someone reading only that line: (1) the question can be answered using only the passage above it; (2) the vocabulary is within the Grade 4 Urdu word list; (3) exactly one of the four options is correct; (4) the question asks for recall or inference, not literary analysis. Then he re-grades all 40 as four checkboxes per row instead of one number. Question #12 now reads: passage-answerable YES, vocabulary YES, one-correct-option YES, recall-or-inference NO — 3 of 4, and the failing box is named. He and his teammate re-grade independently and now agree on 38 of 40; the 2 they still disagree on are both on criterion 2, which sends them to look up what the Grade 4 word list actually contains.
research.failure_mode: The rubric still breaks if a criterion is not independently checkable. Ali's first draft of criterion 4 read 'the question is at the right cognitive level' — which is the same fog as 'quality', just wearing a lab coat. Four boxes of vagueness is worse than one honest number, because the checkboxes make it LOOK measured. The other way it breaks: a criterion that two graders can only agree on by talking to each other. If Ali's teammate has to ask 'what did you mean by right level?', that line is not a criterion yet, it is a conversation. Test each line by handing it to someone cold and seeing whether they can answer without asking a question back.
research.payoff: Ali can now hand the model team a defect report instead of an average: '31 of 40 questions fail criterion 4 — the model keeps asking for literary analysis.' That is one prompt change, retestable against the same four boxes tomorrow. He can also hand the rubric to a second grader, or to a model grader, and get scores he can compare — because the rubric, not the person, is doing the judging.
misconceptions: 'A rubric is just a scoring scale (1-5, or 1-10).' No — the scale is the least important part. A rubric is the list of named checks; the number is what falls out of them
'A more detailed rubric is a better rubric.' No — 12 criteria that nobody applies consistently is worse than 4 that everyone does. Independently checkable beats comprehensive

'I know what I mean by good quality, so writing it down is bureaucracy.' The point is not that Ali does not know — it is that his knowledge is not transferable, not repeatable, and not comparable across two graders or two weeks
'If two graders disagree, the rubric failed.' The opposite: a rubric that surfaces disagreement on a named criterion has done its job. Silent agreement on a vague number is the failure
'Rubrics are for human graders; a model judge does not need one.' A model judge needs it more — a rubric is the only thing standing between you and a model that scores on vibes at scale

script.subtopic: What a Rubric Actually Does

reasons: 21 beats, inside the 16-22 house range; single protagonist named Ali throughout, one running scenario (grading forty AI-generated Urdu reading questions) followed in depth — no domain-hopping.
Exactly one concept: what a rubric actually is (a specification of the judgement, written before you look).

Arc runs in order — friction (01-05 disagreement, 08 self-drift), fix (10-12 he writes the four lines first), structure (11, 13, 14 named criteria), failure mode (17-19 rubber-worded criteria / fog boxes), payoff (15, 20, 21).
Every vo is a single sentence and reads naturally aloud; no beat is a title card.
Both two-person compositions (05, 16) correctly use `scene`, not `ali`; every `ali` beat (01, 07, 10, 17) is a single subject with a whole, non-dividing prop.

No art prompt requests text, letters, numbers, labels or signage — all props are explicitly blank, and every prompt carries the flat 2D vector / plain cream / no ground / no shadow / no desk / no dark fill clause.
Ali is described identically in all ten art prompts (twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, teal collared shirt, dark trousers).

Info-card data is consistent and would render: gauge 17/40 then 38/40 (17 disagreed = 23 agreed at beat 04, 38 agreed at beat 15 — an improvement, not a contradiction), twocard/checks/statement/quote all have their required fields populated and short enough not to overflow.
Only minor fixes remain, all wording-level — the video works as written.

NOTE: the house rule requires an in-video interactive QUESTION → REVEAL using the `quiz` info template with `holdAfter` on the question beat. Beat 18 is written as a question ("Which of these is a criterion yet?") but uses `twocard` and has no `holdAfter`, so there is no pause for the viewer to answer. Flagged as a fix below; graded minor rather than blocker because the beat still renders correctly and teaches the same point, but you may want to convert it before render if that rule is being enforced as non-negotiable.

fixes.problem: This is the script's only question-shaped beat, but it uses the `twocard` template with both answers already visible and no `holdAfter`, so the viewer never gets a beat of silence to answer — the mandatory QUESTION → REVEAL interaction is not actually interactive.
fixes.suggested: Split into two beats: an 18a `info` beat using the `quiz` template with the question "Which of these is a criterion yet?" and the four candidate lines as options, plus `holdAfter` (~2s) so the viewer commits; then keep the current `twocard` as 18b for the reveal. If beat count must stay at 21, fold beat 19's point into 18b's `sub` and reuse its slot.

fixes.problem: The statement text "Raise the average from 3.1 to 4 names no defect" is grammatically compressed — a viewer reading it fast may parse "names" as a noun and stall.
fixes.suggested: Reword to "'Raise the average from 3.1 to 4' names no defect" — wrapping the quoted instruction in quote marks makes "names" unambiguously the verb.

fixes.problem: "A rubber-worded criterion" is a coined phrase the learner meets for the first time here, in the same sentence that also gives an instruction — two new things at once.
fixes.suggested: Split the load: "A criterion made of rubber words stretches to fit whatever the grader already believed." Then let beat 18 carry the instruction to test each line cold.

fixes.problem: Overlay says "31 of 40 fail criterion 4" but the four criteria in beat 11 are unnumbered in the visual, so "criterion 4" asks the viewer to count back six beats.
fixes.suggested: Change the overlay to name the defect instead of numbering it, e.g. "31 of 40: vocabulary above Grade 4" — that matches the vo's "a named defect" literally.

fixes.problem: The vo says "three boxes passed and one box failed", but the art has the failing box as "the lowest one", which reads as criterion 4 — fine, though the overlay "the failing box has a name" does not tell the viewer which name.
fixes.suggested: Optional: change the overlay to the actual failing criterion ("vocabulary above the Grade 4 list") so the promise of a name is kept in the same beat that makes it.

fixes.problem: "Four boxes of fog" leans on "boxes" from beat 14 and "fog" as a fresh metaphor in one breath; the sentence is also the longest in the script.
fixes.suggested: Tighten to "Four vague boxes are worse than one honest number, because they look measured." The overlay "vagueness in a lab coat" already carries the image.

research.topic: What a rubric actually does in an eval — turning a vague quality judgement into a fixed set of observable checks that different graders apply the same way
research.slo: The learner can take a vague quality standard ("is this answer good?") and rewrite it as a rubric of observable, independently-checkable criteria that two different graders would score identically.
research.audience: Content and product people at Taleemabad who are starting to evaluate AI outputs. They have seen an eval run and know an eval means checking outputs against expectations (evals-01 to evals-04). They have never written a rubric and currently judge outputs by gut feel. No coding assumed.
key_points: A rubric is not a scoring form or a grade — it is the written definition of what "good" means for one specific task, in terms a second person could apply without asking you what you meant.
Each criterion must be observable in the output itself: you can point at the text and say yes or no. "Correct grade level" is observable; "feels appropriate" is not.
A rubric splits one blurry judgement into a few independent checks, so a failing output tells you WHICH part failed, not just that it scored low.
The rubric's real job is agreement: the test of a rubric is that two graders scoring the same output land on the same result — not that the score looks impressive.

This video covers what a rubric does and why criteria must be observable and independent; HOW to write and word the criteria line by line is the next video (evals-05), and this SLO only needs the "what it does" half.
research.ali_scenario: Ali is checking an AI assistant that writes Grade 4 Urdu reading-comprehension questions from a story passage. He generates 20 questions from the same passage about a boy who loses his goat, and has to decide which ones are usable in a real worksheet.
research.friction: Ali reads each of the 20 questions and marks them out of 5 by feel — he gives question 3 a 4, question 7 a 2, and so on, ending with an average of 3.4. Then Sara on his team grades the same 20 with the same 0–5 scale and averages 2.1. Neither can explain the gap: Ali counted a two-part question as fine because a teacher could split it, Sara marked it down because it confuses a nine-year-old. When Ali asks the AI to improve, he can only say "make them better," the next batch scores 3.6, and he cannot tell whether anything actually improved or he was just in a better mood on Tuesday.
research.fix: Ali stops scoring the whole question and writes down four things he can literally point at in the text: (1) the answer appears in the passage, not from outside knowledge; (2) it asks exactly one thing — no "and" joining two questions; (3) every word is on the Grade 4 vocabulary list; (4) it is not answerable with just yes or no. He re-grades the 20 questions as four yes/no checks each instead of one gut number. Sara grades the same 20 with the same four checks. They now agree on 19 of 20, and the one they disagree on exposes a criterion that was still vague — "Grade 4 vocabulary" — which Ali pins to a specific word list. The counts also tell him where the model is actually weak: 15 of 20 pass the passage-grounding check, but only 8 pass the one-thing check, so he fixes the prompt for compound questions specifically.
research.failure_mode: Ali gets excited and stretches the rubric to eleven criteria, several of them overlapping ("single question," "not compound," "clear") and one still subjective ("engaging for children"). Grading 20 outputs now takes an hour, and the overlapping criteria triple-punish the same flaw so one compound question drops three checks and looks like a catastrophe, while "engaging" quietly reintroduces the Ali-vs-Sara disagreement he just eliminated. A rubric with more criteria is not a better rubric — every criterion has to be observable and non-overlapping, or it adds noise instead of signal.
research.payoff: Ali can now hand the four checks to anyone on the team — or to an automated grader — and get the same verdict he would have given himself, and he can say precisely what to fix: not "make them better" but "8 of 20 ask two things at once." His before/after comparisons become real evidence instead of a mood, because the standard stopped living in his head and started living on paper.
misconceptions: That a rubric is the numeric score or the star rating — the number is the output; the rubric is the definition of what earns it.
That a rubric is only for grading humans, like a teacher's marking sheet, and has nothing to do with testing an AI system.
That a rubric must be long and exhaustive to be rigorous — four sharp observable checks beat twenty vague ones.
That criteria like "clear," "helpful," or "high quality" are usable criteria; they are just the original vague judgement wearing a rubric's clothes.
That once a rubric is written it is fixed forever — disagreement between graders is the signal that a criterion needs sharpening, not that a grader is wrong.

Arc order holds: friction (01-08 gut scoring, unexplainable 3.4 vs 2.1 gap, 'make them better') -> fix (09-11 observable checks) -> structure (10, 14, 17 the four checks applied and what the counts reveal) -> failure mode (18-19 eleven overlapping criteria) -> payoff (20-22 transferable standard).

Four minor improvements are also listed; none of them block. Fix the two blockers and this is READY.

research.topic: AI in 2030 — why the bottleneck moves from model capability to verification of AI output
research.slo: Given an AI system that is more capable than the human reviewing it, the learner can explain why the reviewer's job shifts from producing work to designing checks that catch wrong work, and can name one check that survives an AI that is confidently wrong.
research.audience: Taleemabad L&D and product people, and teachers-turned-content-builders, who already use AI assistants day to day and have heard '2030 predictions' talk. They know prompting; they have never had to verify output they could not personally have produced.
key_points: This video teaches ONE concept: verification becomes the scarce skill when the AI is faster and broader than you. The other candidate concept in 'AI in 2030' — capability forecasting / timelines — is deliberately not taught, because the SLO is about what the learner DOES, not about predicting dates.
By 2030 the cheap thing is production of plausible work; the expensive thing is knowing whether that work is right. Cost curves invert what a knowledge worker's day looks like.
'It reads well' is not a check. Plausibility is exactly what a strong model optimises, so fluency carries zero information about correctness.
A real check is one the AI cannot satisfy by writing better prose: it hits ground truth outside the AI's output — a source you open, a number you recompute, a sample you spot-inspect.
You cannot verify everything, so you verify where being wrong is most costly and hardest to detect later — that choice is the actual skill.
Checks must be decided BEFORE you see the output; deciding after means you grade against what you were handed.
research.ali_scenario: Ali, a curriculum lead at Taleemabad in 2030, is handed one task with a Friday deadline: publish a Grade 5 maths practice set of 120 questions for the new term. His AI assistant generates all 120 questions with answer keys, worked solutions, difficulty tags and Urdu translations in about 40 seconds. He has roughly two hours before he has to ship. 120 items, 2 hours — about one minute per item if he tried to do all of them, which he cannot.
research.friction: Ali does what feels responsible: he starts reading the questions from the top. They are excellent — clean wording, sensible difficulty ramp, tidy Urdu. He reads 30, finds nothing wrong, feels the deadline, and ships all 120 on the strength of 'the ones I read were fine.' Two weeks later a teacher reports that question 87 asks for the area of a rectangle but the answer key gives the perimeter, and question 103's Urdu translation says 'subtract' where the English says 'divide.' Both read perfectly. Ali's reading pass could never have caught them, because he was checking whether the questions sounded like good questions — the one thing the model was guaranteed to get right. He had spent his two hours confirming fluency and had no evidence at all about correctness.
research.fix: Before opening the output, Ali writes down what could be wrong and how he would know, then spends his two hours only on those. He picks three checks. One: recompute — he solves 12 items himself, chosen not at random but 12 where the answer is a number he can recheck in ten seconds, and compares to the key; question 87's mismatch surfaces on item four. Two: cross-language diff — he has the AI back-translate all 40 Urdu items to English and he scans only for verbs that changed, which catches 103 in under a minute. Three: distribution — he counts how many items land in each difficulty tag and finds 71 of 120 tagged 'medium', a shape no real practice set has. Each check touches ground truth the AI's writing cannot fake: arithmetic he redid, a word-level mismatch between two versions, a count. He ships with 3 known defects fixed and a note on what he did and did not check.
research.failure_mode: The checks quietly stop being checks. Ali reuses the same three every term, the AI's next version learns to produce clean back-translations and a pretty difficulty histogram, and now his checks pass on output he has not actually verified — he is measuring the things that got easy while the errors moved to pedagogy, to whether a question is worth asking at all. Worse, he starts letting the AI run the checks and report 'all clear', which makes the checker and the thing being checked the same system. A check only works while it hits something outside the model's output and while it still sometimes fails; a check that never fails has become a ritual, and Ali has to keep asking what a wrong item would look like NOW, not last term.
research.payoff: Ali can now ship work he did not personally produce and cannot personally reproduce, and still say honestly what he knows about it — 'I recomputed 12, I diffed the translations, I checked the difficulty spread; I did not check pedagogical value.' That sentence is what makes him useful in 2030. He is no longer competing with the AI on output speed, a race he loses; he is doing the part it cannot do for itself — deciding what would count as wrong, and going and looking. It also scales: 1,200 items would not take ten times longer, because checks are chosen by risk, not by volume.
misconceptions: 'When the models get good enough in 2030, verification stops mattering.' It matters more — you verify precisely because you can no longer tell by looking, and the volume you're accountable for goes up.
'Spot-checking means reading a random sample.' Reading is not checking. A sample you only read tells you the output is fluent, which you already knew.
'The AI can check its own work if I ask it to.' It can, and it will agree with itself. A check needs a source of truth the generating system does not control.
'If I can't review all of it, reviewing some of it is meaningless.' Targeted partial checks with a stated scope are the working method; unbounded reading is what's meaningless.
'2030 AI means the job disappears.' The producing part shrinks; the deciding-what-good-means part grows, and it is the part nobody has automated.

reasons: One protagonist named Ali, one running scenario (a Grade Five maths practice set) followed from friction through payoff — no list of separate domain examples.
Exactly one concept: verification is the scarce skill, and a real check must be something plausible-sounding output cannot pass and the model cannot run on itself.

Arc runs in order: friction (01-08 shipped on a read-through and an error came back), fix (11-12 write the checks before opening the output), structure (13-16 the three checks), failure mode (17-18 the AI running its own checks), payoff (19-22).
All 22 beats are within the 16-22 house range; every vo is a single sentence; no title cards.
Every 'ali' beat (01, 05, 10) has a single subject with props detached and floating; every multi-object or second-person composition is correctly 'scene'.

No art prompt requests text, letters, numbers, labels or signage; all specify flat 2D vector on plain cream with no ground, shadow, desk, scenery or dark fill; Ali is described identically in all 16 art prompts.
Mandatory in-video QUESTION -> REVEAL is present: beat 17 asks with a quiz-style checks card, beat 18 reveals.
Info-card data is short and within template shape; the gauge on 16 carries value 71 against max 120 with a good marker at 40, matching the spoken line.
Remaining fixes are minor only — wording length on a few beats and one holdAfter nicety. None block production.

fixes.problem: The question beat carries the quiz content but the script does not show a `holdAfter` on it, so the reveal may land before the viewer has answered.
fixes.suggested: Add `"holdAfter": 3` (or the house default) to beat 17 so the four options stay on screen before beat 18 reveals 'None of them'.

fixes.problem: The sentence is the longest in the script (two clauses plus a timing claim) and may feel rushed at the measured pace.
fixes.suggested: Trim to 'He back-translates the Urdu and scans only for verbs that changed, catching one in under a minute.'

fixes.problem: The em-dash mid-sentence can read as a hard stop in TTS.
fixes.suggested: Replace the dash with a comma: 'You are not competing with the machine on output, you are deciding what would count as wrong and going to look.'

fixes.problem: The statement card's `hi` is '120' while the card text spells the number as a numeral too, so the highlight adds little emphasis.
fixes.suggested: Set `hi` to 'Two hours' so the highlight lands on the scarce resource rather than repeating the count.

fixes.problem: The vo is slightly abstract ('information the model could never have handed him') right after a concrete beat, which softens the moment.
fixes.suggested: Consider 'What that colleague pushes back on is something the model was never in a position to tell him.'

fixes.problem: Beat 17 uses `tpl: "checks"` for the quiz; the house pattern for the interactive question is the `quiz` template.
fixes.suggested: Switch to `"tpl": "quiz"` with the same four options if the quiz template is available, so the question renders in the established QUESTION -> REVEAL styling.

**Visuals** 0.8 — cannot be seen; scored from beat plan only (good info/scene/ali mix, 6 varied info templates, no text-heavy beats). Not verifiable from evidence.

research.topic: Why a written checklist beats a careful reader: turning "I'll just read the output and see if it's good" into a fixed, named list of pass/fail checks applied identically to every sample
research.slo: After this video, the learner can convert a vague "does this output look good?" judgement into a written checklist of 4-6 independent pass/fail checks and explain why the checklist catches failures that careful reading misses.
research.audience: L&D and ops people building their first AI evaluations. They can write a prompt and read an AI output, and they know an eval is "grading the AI", but they judge outputs by feel and have never written down what they are actually checking.
key_points: Careful reading is not repeatable: the same reader applies different standards to sample 1 and sample 40, because attention and mood drift while the output does not.
A checklist externalises the standard into named, written checks, so every sample is judged against the identical bar and two different people reach the same verdict.

Each check must be independent and pass/fail on its own — 'is this good?' is one fused judgement; 'has the child's name', 'has a date', 'no English words', 'under 60 words', 'action the parent can do today' are five separate ones.

The checklist's real power is bookkeeping, not intelligence: it turns 40 vague impressions into a countable grid, so you can say which check fails and how often instead of 'roughly a quarter felt off'.
A checklist makes a failure diagnosable — a column that fails 18 out of 40 times names the defect to fix; a reader's 'these felt weak' names nothing.
This video is about why the checklist beats the reader, not about how to write the perfect check wording — that is the next concept.
research.ali_scenario: Ali is reviewing AI-generated parent-messages for Taleemabad. The prompt takes a pupil's weekly attendance and quiz score and writes a short Urdu WhatsApp message to the parent. He has 40 sample outputs in a spreadsheet, one per pupil, and a Friday afternoon to decide whether this prompt is safe to send to 3,000 parents.
research.friction: Ali reads all 40 messages carefully, one after another, marking each 'good' or 'bad' in a single column by feel. He passes 34 and flags 6. His standard drifts as he goes: message 3 gets rejected for having no date, while message 29 — also with no date — gets waved through because by then he is reading for tone and has stopped noticing dates at all. When his manager asks 'what exactly is wrong with the 6?', all Ali can say is 'they felt off'. When she re-reads the same 40 herself she passes 31, and there is no way to tell which of them is right, because neither wrote down what 'good' meant. Ali re-reads the batch from the top and gets a third answer.
research.fix: Before opening a single output, Ali writes down what a good message must contain, as five checks, each answerable yes/no without reading the others: (1) names the child, (2) states the attendance number, (3) gives one action the parent can do this week, (4) fully in Urdu, no English words, (5) 60 words or fewer. He makes them five columns in the spreadsheet and goes down the sheet check by check — all 40 rows for 'names the child', then all 40 for 'in Urdu' — instead of forming one overall impression per message. The result is a grid of 200 yes/no marks, not 40 feelings. The 'gives one action' column fails 18 times out of 40, which is now the single defect to fix in the prompt, and his manager applying the same five checks to the same 40 rows agrees on 197 of the 200 marks.
research.failure_mode: The checklist still lies if it is applied carelessly. If Ali writes a check as vaguely as his old instinct — 'is the tone warm?' — the drift comes straight back wearing a checkbox, because two people fill that column differently. If he lets checks overlap ('mentions attendance' and 'includes the numbers'), one defect gets counted twice and looks bigger than it is. And a full green row only means the message passed the five things he thought of on Friday: a message that opens with the wrong pupil's name from the row above still scores 5/5, because 'right child' was never a check. A checklist bounds a known standard; it does not notice what the standard omitted.
research.payoff: Ali can hand his manager a grid instead of an opinion: 40 samples, five checks, and one column failing 18 times. The prompt gets one targeted edit — an explicit 'end with one action the parent can take this week' — and the same checklist re-run on 40 fresh outputs shows that column at 2 failures, which is a measured improvement rather than a hunch that it reads better now. Anyone else on the team can run the identical check on next month's batch and get a comparable number.
misconceptions: 'I read carefully, so I don't need a checklist' — the checklist is not there to make you more attentive, it is there to make you consistent across samples and interchangeable with other reviewers.
'A checklist means dumbing the judgement down' — the thinking moves earlier, into deciding what the checks are; the reading step is the part that should be mechanical.
'If the checklist misses something, checklists don't work' — an incomplete checklist is still repeatable and fixable by adding a check; an impression is neither.
'More checks means a better eval' — 20 overlapping checks double-count one defect and hide which failure actually matters; 4-6 independent ones diagnose it.
'The checklist replaces human judgement' — a full green row means the output passed the checks that exist, not that it is good.

research.topic: Why a written checklist beats a careful human reader when judging AI output — the case for a fixed, explicit eval rubric over holistic "does this look good?" review
research.slo: Given a batch of AI-generated outputs to judge, the learner can convert their implicit sense of "good" into a fixed written checklist of independently-checkable items, and explain why that checklist catches failures a careful read-through misses.
research.audience: L&D and product people at Taleemabad who are already using an AI assistant to generate learner-facing content and are eyeballing its output before shipping. They know what a prompt is and have opinions about quality; they have never written an eval rubric and assume careful reading is the highest standard available.
key_points: A careful reader judges holistically: one overall feeling of "good" or "off" — a checklist forces that feeling apart into separate items each answered independently.
Attention is a moving spotlight: whatever the reader is currently worried about gets checked, and everything else silently passes. The checklist is what keeps the un-worried-about items in view.
A checklist makes the standard stable across items and across days — the same output gets the same verdict at 9am and 6pm, from Ali or from a colleague.
Each item must be checkable without judgement: 'has a worked example with real numbers' passes or fails; 'is engaging' just re-imports the vibe the checklist was meant to replace.
Failures become countable — 'the answer key is wrong in 6 of 40' is a fixable pattern; 'the batch felt sloppy' is not.

The topic contains two ideas — writing a rubric, and automating the grading of it. This video covers only the first: turning implicit judgement into an explicit written checklist. Automation is a later video and the SLO does not need it.
research.ali_scenario: Ali is reviewing 40 AI-generated Grade 5 maths word problems for the fractions unit before they go into the LMS. He opens them in one long document at 9:00am, coffee at his elbow, and reads every single one, top to bottom, marking a green tick in the margin. He finishes at 11:20am with 38 ticks and 2 rewrites, and sends the batch to publish.
research.friction: Three days later a teacher WhatsApps a photo of question 27: 'Sara ate 3/4 of a pizza and gave 1/2 to her brother.' The pieces don't add up — the answer key says 1/4 remaining, which is impossible. Ali goes back and re-reads the batch, this time hunting for arithmetic. He finds four more broken answer keys, and nine problems that all use the same pizza-and-brother setup, and three that use words no Grade 5 reader has met. He read every one of these questions carefully three days ago and ticked them. The problem is not that he was lazy — it's that at 9:00am he was reading for 'does this sound like a maths question', and by question 27 he was reading for nothing at all. His attention moved; his standard moved with it. He can't say which 38 he actually checked for what.
research.fix: Ali stops reading and writes the standard down first. Five lines on a sheet of paper, each answerable yes/no without thinking hard: (1) does the arithmetic in the answer key actually resolve; (2) is the context different from the previous question's context; (3) is every word in the Grade 5 vocabulary list; (4) is exactly one fraction operation required; (5) is there a single unambiguous correct answer. Then he changes the shape of the work: instead of reading each problem once against all five, he makes a 40-row grid and does one column at a time — all 40 arithmetic checks, then all 40 context checks. Now what he is looking for cannot drift between question 3 and question 27, because he is only ever looking for one thing. The five broken keys and the nine repeated pizzas both fall out of column 1 and column 2 — and the count, 5/40 and 9/40, tells him the generation prompt is the thing to fix, not the 14 questions.
research.failure_mode: The checklist quietly turns back into vibes when its items aren't independently checkable. Ali's second draft has 'is the question engaging?' as item 6 — and that item passes everything he already likes and fails everything he already dislikes, exactly like the original read-through, but now wearing a tick-box and looking rigorous. The other way it breaks: the checklist only sees what its items name. Ali's five items say nothing about cultural fit, so a problem about counting slices of Christmas ham sails through all five green ticks. A checklist is a promise about coverage, and it only covers what someone wrote on it — so every real failure that gets past it must be added as a new line, or it will get past it again next month.
research.payoff: Ali can now hand the same sheet to a colleague and get the same verdict on the same batch — the standard lives outside his head. He can say 'this batch fails on 5 answer keys and 9 duplicate contexts' instead of 'this batch felt off', which points at the prompt rather than at 40 individual rewrites. And when a new failure arrives from a teacher, he doesn't re-read 40 questions hoping to spot it — he adds a sixth line and re-runs one column.
misconceptions: 'A checklist is for people who aren't careful.' The opposite: it exists because careful attention is a spotlight that moves, and the checklist is what holds the beam still. Ali was careful and still missed 5 broken answer keys.
'Reading the whole thing gives you a fuller picture than ticking boxes.' Holistic reading gives you one merged verdict; the checklist gives you five separate ones you can act on individually.

'Writing the checklist is the slow part.' The re-read after the teacher's complaint cost Ali more time than writing five lines would have — and produced a worse result, because he was still only hunting for the one failure he'd been told about.
'Longer checklist = better checklist.' An item that can't be answered yes/no without judgement adds no coverage and hides the fact that it added none.
'Once written, it's finished.' The checklist only catches what's written on it; every new escaped failure is a new line.

Exactly one concept: a written checklist applied column-wise beats careful reading, because attention drifts.

20 beats, inside the 16-22 house range; every vo is a single sentence and reads aloud naturally.

Cutout safety is clean: the only `ali` beat (08) is propless; every beat where a prop must move is `scene`.

Ali is described identically in all ten art prompts (young Pakistani man, twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, teal collared shirt, dark trousers) and every prompt specifies flat 2D vector on plain cream with no ground, shadow, desk or dark fill, and forbids text.

topic: how do I use WhatsApp for my shop

interventions.detail: gate sent it back to script (round 1/8).

research.topic: Using WhatsApp Business as the order-taking and follow-up channel for a small physical shop — specifically, turning scattered chat messages into a single trackable order flow using a catalogue, labels, and saved quick replies
research.slo: After this video, the learner can set up a WhatsApp Business catalogue and label system so that every customer enquiry becomes a trackable order with a known status, instead of a message that gets lost in the chat list.
research.audience: Small shop owners and shop staff in Pakistan who already use WhatsApp daily on a personal phone to chat with customers, know how to send photos and voice notes, but have never used WhatsApp Business features (catalogue, labels, quick replies, away message) and have no other order-tracking system.
key_points: A shop chat thread is not an order record — an order needs an item, a price, a status, and a name attached to it, and plain WhatsApp gives you none of those.
The catalogue turns 'what do you have?' into a link you send once: item photo, name, and price live in one place, so you stop re-typing prices and stop quoting different prices to different people.
Labels are the status field a chat list does not have — New Order / Paid / Packed / Delivered — and they let you filter 40 chats down to only the ones needing action today.
Quick replies (/shipping, /price, /timings) make your most-repeated answers one keystroke, which is what keeps the system alive on a busy day.

The topic contains two teachable concepts — (a) presenting the shop via catalogue and (b) tracking orders via labels. This video teaches the tracking system, because the SLO is about orders not getting lost; the catalogue is taught only as the input that feeds it.
The system only works if the label is moved at the moment the physical thing happens — labelling later, from memory, is how the whole thing rots.
research.ali_scenario: Ali runs a one-room cloth shop in Gujranwala — Ali Fabrics — with a printed lawn suit stack behind him and a phone on a charging cable by the counter. It is the Thursday before Eid. Between 9am and 2pm his phone takes 43 WhatsApp messages from customers about the same three items: the blue lawn 3-piece at Rs 4,200, the green at Rs 3,800, and the embroidered white at Rs 6,500. We follow Ali through this one Thursday and into Friday morning, when the courier boy arrives at 11am to collect the day's parcels.
research.friction: Ali answers every message by scrolling up to find the price, re-typing 'Rs 4200, blue lawn, delivery Rs 250 extra', and photographing the same suit again for the eleventh time. Orders live only in his head and in the chat list. At 2pm he has 43 unread-or-half-read chats and no way to see which of them actually owe him money. A customer named Sana sent Rs 4,200 on Easypaisa at 11:40am; her message is now buried 30 chats down, so on Friday the courier leaves with 6 parcels and hers is not one of them. Ali also quoted the green suit at Rs 3,800 to one customer and Rs 4,000 to another because he was going from memory, and the second customer screenshots both and asks why.
research.fix: Ali switches to WhatsApp Business and does three things before opening the shop on Friday. He builds a catalogue with the three suits — real photo, exact name, exact price typed once — so every 'kya rate hai?' is answered by sending the catalogue item instead of a fresh photo and a fresh typed price. He creates four labels: New Order, Paid, Packed, Delivered. And he saves three quick replies — /rate, /delivery, /timings. Then he works the day by rule: the moment a customer says yes, the chat gets New Order; the moment the Easypaisa screenshot lands, it moves to Paid; the moment Ali tapes the parcel shut, Packed; the moment the courier takes it, Delivered. At 10:50am Friday, before the courier arrives, he filters by Paid and gets a list of exactly 7 chats — Sana's now among them — and packs from that list instead of from memory.
research.failure_mode: Ali starts batching the labelling — he tells himself he will label 'after Zuhr' — and by Saturday he has 12 chats sitting on New Order that are actually paid, plus two marked Paid that were only 'I will send money tonight'. The label list now lies, so he stops trusting it and goes back to scrolling. The same rot happens the other way: he adds 14 labels (New, Maybe, Asked Price, Thinking, Paid Half, Paid Full...) and the filter no longer narrows anything. The system survives only on a short label set moved at the physical moment — payment received, parcel taped, courier gone — not on a tidy-up session later.
research.payoff: Ali can now stand at his counter at 10:50am, tap one filter, and see every order that is paid and not yet packed — a list, not a memory. He stops quoting two prices for one suit, stops re-photographing stock, and hands the courier a stack that matches the money he has actually received. On the next Eid rush he can hand the phone to his younger brother for two hours and the brother can work the same list, because the status is on the screen instead of in Ali's head.
misconceptions: That WhatsApp Business is a separate paid app or requires a new phone number — it is free and can run on the same number, or a second number on the same phone.
That switching to WhatsApp Business loses your existing chats and customers — the chats transfer over.
That the catalogue is only for big sellers with hundreds of items — three items priced correctly already stops the re-typing and the price contradictions.
That labels are just decoration or colour-coding — they are the only status field the app has, and the filter is the actual product.
That more labels means better tracking — a long label list is what makes the filter useless.
That a pinned chat or a starred message does the same job as a label — pinning keeps a chat at the top but tells you nothing about whether it is paid or packed.

reasons: One protagonist, Ali, in one running scenario — his Eid-rush cloth shop — followed from Thursday friction to Friday payoff; the courier and Sana are supporting figures, never second protagonists, and every beat that shows a second person is correctly `scene`.
Exactly one concept: a chat thread has no status field, so orders must be given one. The catalogue is a supporting step, not a second concept.
Arc runs in order: friction (01-06), diagnosis and fix (07-10), structure and rule (11-14), question and failure modes (15-17), payoff (18-20).
20 beats, inside the 16-22 house range; every `vo` is one sentence and reads naturally aloud; no title cards.

Interactive question present and correct: beat 15 is mode info / tpl quiz with holdAfter 2 and a spoken question, and beat 16 answers it. The answer ('labelling later, from memory') is earned by beats 12-13, not a definition recall.

Real numbers on screen: five distinct data templates (bignum 02, bars 04, piles 11, scoresheet 16, gauge 17) carrying actual figures, and only two text cards (07, 13). Numbers are internally consistent — 43 customers in 02 is the gauge max in 17, and the 7 Paid in the piles of 11 is the exact 7 Ali filters to in 19.

All art prompts are flat 2D vector on plain cream, with no ground, shadow, desk, scenery or dark fill; all forbid text, letters, numbers, labels and signage; Ali is described identically in every prompt (twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, teal collared shirt, dark trousers).
Both `ali` beats (10, 18) have a single subject and hold only a phone contiguous with the hand — nothing that must move independently, so the cutout is safe.
Every scene prompt names a physical act (photographing, swiping, handing over, passing, setting down, taping, pointing, lifting) rather than only a mood.

topic: how do I use WhatsApp for my shop

interventions.detail: gate sent it back to script (round 1/8).

research.topic: Using WhatsApp Business as the order-taking and follow-up system for a small retail shop — specifically, using a saved product catalogue plus quick replies so every customer enquiry ends in a confirmed order instead of a lost chat
research.slo: After this video, the learner can set up a WhatsApp Business catalogue and quick replies so that a customer enquiry is answered with price, availability, and a confirmable order summary in under a minute, without retyping.
research.audience: Small shopkeepers and home-business owners in Pakistan who already use WhatsApp daily for personal chats and receive customer messages there, but have never used WhatsApp Business, a catalogue, or any saved-reply feature. They know how to send a message, a photo, and a voice note. They do not know what a 'business profile', 'catalogue', or 'quick reply' is.
key_points: WhatsApp Business is a separate free app from regular WhatsApp; the shop's number moves into it and all old chats come along, so nothing is lost
The catalogue is a one-time cost: each item is entered once with a photo, a name, and a price, and from then on it is sent as a card in two taps instead of retyped
A quick reply is a saved block of text triggered by typing '/' plus a shortcut — it turns the answers you repeat twenty times a day into one keystroke

The point is not speed for its own sake: a reply that arrives with price + availability + a written order summary is what converts an enquiry into a confirmed order, because the customer never has to ask a second question

The order summary must be sent as text in the chat (item, quantity, price, total, delivery, address) so both sides have the same record to point back at — this is what prevents the 'I never said 3, I said 2' fight

This video covers catalogue + quick replies only. WhatsApp Business also has broadcast lists and away messages; those are a separate concept and are deliberately left out so the one outcome above stays achievable
Turning on a business profile (shop name, hours, address) changes nothing about how you chat, but it is what makes the customer trust that the number is a shop and not a stranger
research.ali_scenario: Ali runs a small cloth and ready-made kurta shop in a bazaar lane — one room, shelves stacked with folded kurtas, a glass counter, a phone charging on the counter. It is the last week before Eid. Customers are messaging his shop number all day asking about the same navy-blue embroidered kurta: 'price?', 'medium hai?', 'photo bhejo'. He is following one specific customer, Sana, who messages at 2:14 pm asking about that kurta while he is mid-sale with a walk-in customer at the counter.
research.friction: Ali is on plain WhatsApp with no catalogue and no saved replies. To answer Sana he has to put down the cloth he is folding, scroll up through his own gallery hunting for the navy kurta photo he took last week, find the wrong one twice, send it, then type the price from memory — 'Rs 3,450' — then she asks about medium, he has to walk to the shelf, count, come back and type again. Each enquiry takes him eleven minutes of stop-start attention. By 6 pm he has 23 unanswered messages, he has quoted the same kurta at Rs 3,450 to one customer and Rs 3,200 to another because he was going from memory, and Sana — who waited 40 minutes for the first reply — has stopped answering; she bought it from the shop two doors down. He counts four orders lost that day, roughly Rs 13,000, not because his prices were wrong but because his replies were slow and inconsistent.
research.fix: That night Ali installs WhatsApp Business, moves his shop number over, and fills the profile with the shop name, bazaar address, and hours 10 am–9 pm. Then he does the one-time work: he photographs his 12 best-selling items on the counter under the tube light and enters each into the catalogue — 'Navy Embroidered Kurta, Rs 3,450', with sizes written into the description. Then he writes three quick replies: /price (sends the catalogue item link plus 'Ye rate final hai, Eid tak same'), /size ('Available sizes: S, M, L, XL — bta dein kaun sa chahiye'), and /order (a fill-in template: item, quantity, size, total, delivery charge Rs 150, address). Next morning a customer asks about the same navy kurta. Ali taps the catalogue, sends the card with photo and price attached, types /size, and when she says medium he sends /order filled in: '1 × Navy Embroidered Kurta (M) — Rs 3,450 + delivery Rs 150 = Rs 3,600. Deliver to: ___. Confirm karein?' Fifty-two seconds, without leaving the counter. She confirms.
research.failure_mode: The catalogue goes stale and the quick replies start lying for him. Three weeks later Ali's supplier raises the price to Rs 3,800 and the navy kurta sells out in medium — but the catalogue card still says Rs 3,450 and /size still promises M. Now the saved reply sends a wrong promise faster and more confidently than he ever could by hand, and to more people. A customer confirms an order at Rs 3,450 and shows him the message he himself sent; he either eats Rs 350 or he argues with a customer holding his own written quote. The fix only holds if updating the catalogue price and marking items out-of-stock becomes part of closing the shop each night — the same five minutes he already spends counting the cash box — and if the /order template is always filled in fresh per customer instead of sent with the last customer's quantity still in it.
research.payoff: Ali can now answer an enquiry in under a minute from the counter without stopping the sale in front of him, and every quote he gives is the same price, because it comes from the catalogue instead of his memory. In the three days before Eid he handles 60 enquiries instead of 23 and closes 19 orders. Because each order ends in a written summary both sides can scroll back to, he has zero delivery disputes that week — and because his 12 items are already photographed and priced, a new customer can browse the whole shop from the bazaar road at 11 pm when the shutter is down.
misconceptions: 'WhatsApp Business is a paid app / costs money per message.' — The app and the catalogue are free; Ali pays nothing beyond his normal data.
'I will lose my chats and contacts if I switch.' — The number and chat history transfer over during setup; regular WhatsApp is simply replaced on that phone.
'I need a separate SIM or a new number for a business account.' — The existing shop number can be moved into WhatsApp Business directly.

'Quick replies make me sound like a robot and customers will feel ignored.' — The saved text handles only the repeated facts (price, sizes, delivery charge); Ali still types the human part. It buys him the time to be personal where it matters.
'A catalogue is only for big stores with hundreds of products.' — Twelve items covered most of Ali's enquiries; the catalogue earns its keep on whatever people ask about most, not on size.
'Once the catalogue is set up, the work is done.' — It is a living price list. An un-updated catalogue is worse than no catalogue, because it broadcasts an outdated promise in writing.

options: A fast reply with the catalogue card and price, then waiting for her next question

The catalogue card sent within seconds, because replying first is what wins the customer

topic: how do I price my tailoring work

interventions.detail: gate sent it back to script (round 1/8).

research.topic: How to price tailoring work: costing a stitched garment from materials, labour time, overhead and margin instead of quoting from memory or from what the neighbour charges
research.slo: Given a stitching order, the learner can calculate a price by adding material cost, their own hourly labour cost for measured stitching time, a share of monthly overhead, and a margin — and state why that number is the floor below which the order loses money.
research.audience: Home-based and small-shop tailors in Pakistan who already stitch well and take orders daily, but set prices by habit, haggling, or by copying the shop next door. They can do basic arithmetic on a phone calculator; they have never separated cost from price, and have no idea what an hour of their own time costs.
key_points: The topic contains two possible concepts — how to price (cost-up costing) and how to negotiate/raise prices with customers. The SLO needs the first, so this video teaches cost-up costing only; raising prices with existing customers is a separate video.

A price is built from four stacked parts: materials actually consumed, labour = measured hours x your own hourly rate, a share of monthly overhead (rent, electricity, machine servicing, thread and needles), then margin on top.
Your own time is a cost even though no one invoices you for it — an hourly rate is set by deciding what you need to earn in a month and dividing by the hours you can realistically stitch.
Overhead is monthly and fixed, so it must be divided across the number of garments you actually finish in a month — not guessed per order.
The four parts added together give the floor price; margin is what sits above the floor and is the only part that is profit.
Time must be measured on a real garment with a clock, not remembered, because remembered time is always shorter than real time.
research.ali_scenario: Ali runs a one-man tailoring shop in a lane in Faisalabad with one machine and one overlocker. A regular customer, Mrs. Rashid, brings 4 metres of lawn and asks for one embroidered-neck kameez with piping and lining. Ali has always quoted this kind of kameez at Rs 1,200 because that is what the shop across the lane charges. The whole video follows this one kameez: Ali times himself stitching it, writes down what it consumed, and works out what it actually cost him.
research.friction: Ali quotes Rs 1,200 from memory and gets to work. The kameez takes him two and a half days of real machine time — he clocks 9 hours — plus Rs 180 of lining, Rs 60 of piping, thread and one broken needle. At the end of the month he has stitched 20 garments, collected about Rs 24,000, and after paying Rs 6,000 shop rent, Rs 1,800 electricity and Rs 1,200 for machine servicing and supplies he is left with roughly Rs 15,000 for a month of 180 hours at the machine — about Rs 83 an hour, less than the boy who irons next door. He cannot see where the money went because he has never separated what the cloth and his hours cost from what he charged, and the busiest months feel the poorest.
research.fix: Ali takes a notebook and builds the price of Mrs. Rashid's kameez in four stacked layers instead of recalling a number. Materials he actually used: Rs 180 lining + Rs 60 piping + Rs 30 thread and needle = Rs 270. Labour: he decides he needs Rs 45,000 a month and can genuinely stitch 180 hours, so his rate is Rs 250 an hour; the kameez took a measured 9 hours = Rs 2,250. Overhead: Rs 9,000 of monthly rent, electricity and servicing divided by the 20 garments he finishes in a month = Rs 450 per garment. That is a floor of Rs 2,970. He adds 20% margin and the price becomes Rs 3,564, which he rounds to Rs 3,500 — not Rs 1,200. The same four layers, in the same order, price every order he takes after that.
research.failure_mode: Ali applies the formula but feeds it soft numbers. He estimates the kameez at '4 hours or so' from memory instead of the 9 hours the clock showed, and he divides overhead by the 30 garments he hopes to finish rather than the 20 he actually finishes. Both errors push the same way — downward — so the arithmetic looks rigorous and still lands him near Rs 1,200. The method only protects him if the hours are timed on a real garment and the garment count is last month's real count; an honest formula fed optimistic inputs just dresses up the old guess.
research.payoff: Ali can now put a number on any order before he touches the cloth, and say out loud which layer it came from. He can tell Mrs. Rashid that the embroidered neck adds 3 hours and therefore Rs 750, instead of arguing about Rs 200. He can see that a plain shalwar at Rs 800 is below his floor and either reprice it or decline it, and he can decide that his simple kameez is the order worth taking more of. Same machine, same hands, same lane — he now stitches fewer garments and ends the month with more money.
misconceptions: 'The price is whatever the shop next door charges.' Their rent, speed and garment mix are different; copying their price copies a number that was never calculated for your costs.
'My own labour is free because I own the shop.' Unpaid hours are the largest single cost in a stitched garment; leaving them out guarantees the price is below the floor.
'Materials plus a little extra is the price.' Materials are usually the smallest of the four layers; overhead and labour together are typically several times the cloth cost.

'If I raise my price I will lose every customer.' The 20 garments at a loss-making price are the problem, not the solution — fewer correctly-priced orders can pay more than a full month of underpriced ones.
'Busy months are good months.' Volume at a price below the floor loses money faster; being busy is only good once the floor is known.

Exactly one concept is taught: building a garment price in stacked layers (materials, labour, overhead, margin).
Arc runs in order — friction (01-07), fix (08), structure (09-14), failure mode (16-18), payoff (19-20).
20 beats, inside the 16-22 house range; every vo is one sentence.

The arithmetic holds all the way through and is internally consistent: 24,000 − 9,000 = 15,000; 15,000 − (20 × 270) = 9,600 over 180 hours = Rs 53/hr (beat 06 gauge); 45,000 ÷ 180 = Rs 250/hr (beat 11); 270 + 2,250 + 450 = Rs 2,970 floor (beat 13); +20% = 3,564 → quoted 3,600 (beat 14); 3 hours × 250 = Rs 750 (beat 19). script.title: how do I price my tailoring work

beats.vo: A regular customer hands Ali four metres of lawn and asks for one embroidered-neck kameez.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, standing centred and fully visible, both hands reaching out to receive a folded bolt of pale green cloth held out by an older Pakistani woman in a plain shawl standing beside him, the cloth passing between their hands, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank props

beats.vo: He quotes twelve hundred rupees, because that is what the shop across the lane charges.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, shrugging with one open palm raised and the other thumb jerking over his shoulder, casual confident expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage

beats.vo: The kameez takes him nine real hours at the machine, and he never writes that down.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, seated centred and fully visible, both hands feeding pale green cloth steadily under the needle of a simple sewing machine, a blank round wall clock floating detached beside him, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank clock face
beats.motion: his hands feed the cloth forward under the needle in a slow steady rhythm

beats.vo: At the end of the month he counts twenty finished garments and about twenty-four thousand rupees collected.
Rent, electricity and machine servicing eat nine thousand of it before he pays himself anything.
Fifteen thousand left, minus the cloth and thread he never counted, is under sixty rupees an hour.
That is less than the boy next door earns, and Ali cannot see where the money went.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, holding a small open notebook in one hand and turning both palms upward in confusion, tired puzzled expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank notebook pages

beats.vo: So he stops guessing and builds the price of that one kameez in four stacked layers.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, stacking four blank rectangular cards one on top of another with both hands, the cards floating in a vertical stack in front of him, determined focused expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank cards
beats.motion: the four cards settle into the stack one after another under his hands

beats.vo: Layer one is what the garment actually ate: lining, piping, thread and one broken needle.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, pointing with one finger at a floating row of a small folded lining cloth, a coil of piping cord, a thread spool and a snapped needle, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage

beats.vo: Layer two is his own time, which nobody invoices him for but costs him all the same.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, holding up a blank round wall clock in both hands in front of his chest, serious steady expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank clock face

beats.vo: He needs forty-five thousand a month and can truly stitch a hundred and eighty hours, so his rate is two hundred fifty.

data.note: Ali's hourly rate: Rs 250 — 9 measured hours = Rs 2,250

beats.vo: Layer three is the shop itself: nine thousand of monthly costs split across the twenty garments he finishes.
Those three layers stacked give him a floor of two thousand nine hundred and seventy rupees.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, pressing one flat palm down firmly on top of a stack of three blank rectangular blocks floating in front of him, calm certain expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank blocks
beats.motion: his palm presses down and the three blocks settle firmly together

beats.vo: Margin is the fourth layer, the only part that is profit, and it sits on top of the floor.

data.note: Ali rounds it up and quotes Rs 3,600 — not Rs 1,200

quiz.stem: Ali finishes a plain shalwar: Rs 120 of cloth and thread, 2 measured hours of stitching. What is the lowest price he can charge without losing money?
options: Rs 620 — materials plus his 2 hours at Rs 250
Rs 1,070 — materials, his 2 hours, and Rs 450 of shop overhead
Rs 120 plus whatever the shop next door adds on top
Rs 800 — the price customers in his lane already accept
quiz.explain: Materials plus labour still leaves out the rent, electricity and servicing that run whether or not this shalwar exists, so a price built from only those two layers quietly eats the shop's costs. Every garment must carry its share of the monthly overhead — Rs 9,000 across 20 garments is Rs 450 — which puts the floor at Rs 1,070, and the neighbour's price or the customer's habit tells you nothing about your own costs.

beats.vo: But the method breaks the moment he feeds it numbers he remembered instead of numbers he measured.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, crossing out a line in a small open notebook with a pen held in one hand, the notebook held up in the other hand, frowning slightly, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank notebook pages
beats.motion: the pen strikes a short line across the page and lifts away

beats.vo: He writes four hours instead of nine, and divides by thirty garments he hopes for instead of twenty he finished.

data.note: Both soft numbers push the same way — downward

beats.vo: An honest formula fed optimistic inputs is just the old guess wearing a better shirt.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, holding a small stopwatch up beside his face with one hand and tapping it with a finger of the other, firm knowing expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank stopwatch face

beats.vo: Now he can tell his customer that the embroidered neck adds three hours, and therefore seven hundred fifty rupees.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, standing centred and fully visible, holding out an open notebook toward an older Pakistani woman in a plain shawl beside him and pointing at a line on the page, calm explaining expression, the woman leaning in to look, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank notebook pages

beats.vo: Same machine, same hands, same lane — he now stitches fewer garments and ends the month with more money.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, hanging a finished pale green kameez onto a floating blank hanger with both hands raised, quietly satisfied expression, a simple sewing machine floating detached beside him, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage
beats.motion: he lifts the kameez onto the hanger and it settles, swaying gently

script.title: how do I price my tailoring work

beats.vo: A regular customer hands Ali four metres of lawn and asks for one embroidered-neck kameez.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, standing centred and fully visible, both hands reaching out to receive a folded bolt of pale green cloth held out by an older Pakistani woman in a plain shawl standing beside him, the cloth passing between their hands, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank props

beats.vo: He quotes twelve hundred rupees, because that is what the shop across the lane charges.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, shrugging with one open palm raised and the other thumb jerking over his shoulder, casual confident expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage

beats.vo: The kameez takes him nine real hours at the machine, and he never writes that down.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, seated centred and fully visible, both hands feeding pale green cloth steadily under the needle of a simple sewing machine, a blank round wall clock floating detached beside him, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank clock face
beats.motion: his hands feed the cloth forward under the needle in a slow steady rhythm

beats.vo: At the end of the month he counts twenty finished garments and about twenty-four thousand rupees collected.
Rent, electricity and machine servicing eat nine thousand of it before he pays himself anything.
Fifteen thousand left, minus the cloth and thread he never counted, is under sixty rupees an hour.
That is less than the boy next door earns, and Ali cannot see where the money went.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, holding a small open notebook in one hand and turning both palms upward in confusion, tired puzzled expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank notebook pages

beats.vo: So he stops guessing and builds the price of that one kameez in four stacked layers.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, stacking four blank rectangular cards one on top of another with both hands, the cards floating in a vertical stack in front of him, determined focused expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank cards
beats.motion: the four cards settle into the stack one after another under his hands

beats.vo: Layer one is what the garment actually ate: lining, piping, thread and one broken needle.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, pointing with one finger at a floating row of a small folded lining cloth, a coil of piping cord, a thread spool and a snapped needle, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage

beats.vo: Layer two is his own time, which nobody invoices him for but costs him all the same.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, holding up a blank round wall clock in both hands in front of his chest, serious steady expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank clock face

beats.vo: He needs forty-five thousand a month and can truly stitch a hundred and eighty hours, so his rate is two hundred fifty.

data.note: Ali's hourly rate: Rs 250 — 9 measured hours = Rs 2,250

beats.vo: Layer three is the shop itself: nine thousand of monthly costs split across the twenty garments he finishes.
Those three layers stacked give him a floor of two thousand nine hundred and seventy rupees.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, pressing one flat palm down firmly on top of a stack of three blank rectangular blocks floating in front of him, calm certain expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank blocks
beats.motion: his palm presses down and the three blocks settle firmly together

beats.vo: Margin is the fourth layer, the only part that is profit, and it sits on top of the floor.

data.note: Ali rounds it up and quotes Rs 3,600 — not Rs 1,200

quiz.stem: Ali finishes a plain shalwar: Rs 120 of cloth and thread, 2 measured hours of stitching. What is the lowest price he can charge without losing money?
options: Rs 620 — materials plus his 2 hours at Rs 250
Rs 1,070 — materials, his 2 hours, and Rs 450 of shop overhead
Rs 120 plus whatever the shop next door adds on top
Rs 800 — the price customers in his lane already accept
quiz.explain: Materials plus labour still leaves out the rent, electricity and servicing that run whether or not this shalwar exists, so a price built from only those two layers quietly eats the shop's costs. Every garment must carry its share of the monthly overhead — Rs 9,000 across 20 garments is Rs 450 — which puts the floor at Rs 1,070, and the neighbour's price or the customer's habit tells you nothing about your own costs.

beats.vo: But the method breaks the moment he feeds it numbers he remembered instead of numbers he measured.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, crossing out a line in a small open notebook with a pen held in one hand, the notebook held up in the other hand, frowning slightly, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank notebook pages
beats.motion: the pen strikes a short line across the page and lifts away

beats.vo: He writes four hours instead of nine, and divides by thirty garments he hopes for instead of twenty he finished.

data.note: Both soft numbers push the same way — downward

beats.vo: An honest formula fed optimistic inputs is just the old guess wearing a better shirt.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, holding a small stopwatch up beside his face with one hand and tapping it with a finger of the other, firm knowing expression, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank stopwatch face

beats.vo: Now he can tell his customer that the embroidered neck adds three hours, and therefore seven hundred fifty rupees.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, standing centred and fully visible, holding out an open notebook toward an older Pakistani woman in a plain shawl beside him and pointing at a line on the page, calm explaining expression, the woman leaning in to look, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, blank notebook pages

beats.vo: Same machine, same hands, same lane — he now stitches fewer garments and ends the month with more money.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, clean-shaven, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers, centred and fully visible, hanging a finished pale green kameez onto a floating blank hanger with both hands raised, quietly satisfied expression, a simple sewing machine floating detached beside him, props detached and floating, no ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage
beats.motion: he lifts the kameez onto the hanger and it settles, swaying gently
