research.topic: "broke" — being broke: running out of money before the month runs out, and why it happens even on a steady income
research.interpretation: You typed only the word "broke" with a course-test note, so I read it as the money sense and narrowed it to the single most teachable cause of being broke on a steady income — spending from your account balance instead of from what is actually uncommitted — because that is the one move a learner can do differently the same day.
research.slo: After watching, the learner can calculate their true spendable amount for the rest of a month by subtracting still-due fixed commitments from their current balance, and state that number before making a discretionary purchase.
research.audience: Working adults in Pakistan earning a regular monthly salary into a bank or mobile-wallet account, who can read a balance and do basic arithmetic but have never separated committed money from spendable money; no budgeting or finance background assumed.
key_points: Being broke on a steady income is usually a timing problem, not an earning problem: money that is already owed still shows in the balance.
Your account balance is not your spendable money — spendable = balance minus commitments still due before the next salary.
Fixed commitments (rent, utilities, school fee, instalment, loan repayment) are dated, so you can list them and their dates in under five minutes.
The check is a subtraction done before the purchase, not a record kept after it.

The topic contains two possible concepts — how to spend less, and how to know what you can spend. The SLO needs the second, so this video teaches the balance-minus-commitments check and leaves spending less alone.
A small daily leak drains the same account as the big commitments, so the check must be repeated, not done once on payday.
research.ali_scenario: Ali is a 29-year-old shop supervisor in Lahore paid Rs 62,000 on the 1st of every month into his Easypaisa account. It is the 14th of the month, his app shows Rs 21,400, and his cousin's wedding shopping is that evening — a suit he has been eyeing costs Rs 9,000. He is followed through this single evening and the fourteen days after it.
research.friction: Ali looks only at the Rs 21,400 on his screen, decides Rs 9,000 is comfortably affordable, and buys the suit, leaving Rs 12,400. He has forgotten that his room rent of Rs 14,000 is due on the 20th and the electricity bill of Rs 3,800 on the 22nd — Rs 17,800 of that balance was never his to spend. On the 20th he is Rs 5,400 short, borrows it from his elder brother with an apology, and spends the last week of the month eating at the shop because there is nothing left for anything else. His salary never changed; only his reading of the balance was wrong.
research.fix: Before the next purchase, Ali opens his notes app and writes the commitments still due before the 1st: rent Rs 14,000 on the 20th, electricity Rs 3,800 on the 22nd, his mother's medicine Rs 2,200 on the 25th, and his bike instalment Rs 4,500 on the 28th — Rs 24,500 in total. He subtracts that from his balance. When the balance is Rs 21,400, the subtraction gives minus Rs 3,100: there is no spendable money at all, and the honest answer to the suit is not yet. He waits, and on payday the same subtraction on Rs 62,000 shows Rs 37,500 spendable for the whole month — so he knows the suit costs him a quarter of everything he has to live on, and he buys a Rs 3,500 shirt instead.
research.failure_mode: Ali does the subtraction once on the 1st, writes down Rs 37,500 spendable, and then spends against that number for four weeks without redoing it — so his daily Rs 400 on chai, rides and top-ups quietly eats the same account while the figure in his notes stays frozen at Rs 37,500. By the 19th the note still says he has money and the app says Rs 11,000, and rent is due tomorrow. The subtraction only protects him if he redoes it against the live balance each time he is about to spend, and if every commitment is on the list — the ones he pays in cash and never sees leave the account are the easiest to omit, and omitting one makes the answer confidently wrong rather than roughly wrong.
research.payoff: Ali can look at any balance on any day of the month and say, in ten seconds, what is actually his — so he can say yes to a purchase without dread and no without guessing. He stops borrowing from his brother at month-end, and the last week of the month stops being the week he eats at the shop.
misconceptions: "I'm broke because I don't earn enough" — being short on a salary that covers your commitments is a sequencing problem before it is an income problem.
"The balance in my app is my money" — it includes money already promised to someone else.
"I need a full budget with categories and an app before I can fix this" — one list of dated commitments and one subtraction is the whole method.
"If I can afford it today, I can afford it" — affordability depends on what is due before the next salary, not on today's number.
"Small daily spending doesn't matter next to rent" — Rs 400 a day is Rs 12,000 a month, which is close to Ali's rent.

quiz.stem: It is the 12th. Ali's wallet shows Rs 18,000. Rent of Rs 14,000 is due on the 20th and his bike instalment of Rs 4,500 on the 28th. A friend asks him to split a Rs 3,000 dinner. What should Ali conclude?
options: He can afford it, because Rs 18,000 easily covers a Rs 3,000 dinner today
He has nothing spendable, because his commitments before payday already exceed the balance
He can afford half of it, because the instalment is still two weeks away
He should skip it only if he has no savings set aside for emergencies
quiz.explain: Comparing the Rs 3,000 to today's Rs 18,000 is exactly the mistake that left Ali short — that balance already contains Rs 18,500 of dated payments, so it was never his to spend. A commitment being two weeks away does not make it optional either; the test is everything due before the next salary, not what is due this week.

beats.vo: But there is a trap: Ali does the subtraction once on payday and then trusts that figure for four weeks.

research.topic: "broke" — the state of having run out of money before the month runs out, and the one move that prevents it
research.interpretation: You typed only the word "broke" with a course-test requeue note, so I read it as the everyday money sense and narrowed it to the single teachable move that stops the mid-month cash hole: paying your fixed commitments and a small savings slice on payday, before any spending, rather than trying to save whatever is left at month-end.
research.slo: After this video, the learner can take a single month's income and allocate it on payday — fixed commitments first, a fixed savings slice second, spending last — and state how much is genuinely free to spend that month.
research.audience: Working adults earning a regular monthly salary for the first few years, who know roughly what they earn and what their bills are, but have never written the two down side by side in the same place on the same day.
key_points: "Broke" is usually a timing problem, not an income problem: the money arrived, it just left in the wrong order.
Money spent early in the month is spent against commitments that have not been paid yet, so the shortfall is invisible until the bills land.
A payday allocation reverses the order: commitments and savings are removed from the balance first, and only the remainder is treated as spendable.
The number that matters is not the salary, it is the remainder after commitments — that is the only figure to spend against.
Savings has to be a fixed slice taken on payday, not a leftover, because leftovers are what disappear.
This video teaches allocation, not budgeting categories or cutting expenses — the SLO is about ordering money on payday, so category tracking is deliberately left out.
research.ali_scenario: Ali is a first-year sales coordinator paid Rs 60,000 on the 1st of each month into one account he checks on his phone. His commitments are rent Rs 22,000 (due the 5th), electricity and gas averaging Rs 6,000 (due the 12th), a motorbike installment Rs 7,000 (due the 15th), phone and internet Rs 3,000, and Rs 5,000 he sends home. We follow him through one single month, September, from the morning the salary lands to the 24th.
research.friction: On the morning of the 1st, Ali's app shows Rs 60,000 and he reads that number as what he has. He buys a Rs 9,000 pair of shoes he'd been eyeing, eats out four times in the first week, and lends a friend Rs 4,000. He is not reckless — every one of those felt affordable against 60,000. Then rent takes 22,000 on the 5th, the bike installment 7,000 on the 15th, and by the 18th the balance reads Rs 2,400 with the electricity bill still unpaid and six days of commuting left. He borrows Rs 5,000 from the same friend he lent to, and saves nothing — again.
research.fix: On the 1st of October, before spending a rupee, Ali writes his five commitments on one sheet and adds them: Rs 43,000. He transfers Rs 5,000 into a separate savings account the same morning, and pays or sets aside the commitments he can. Then he does the only subtraction that matters: 60,000 − 43,000 − 5,000 = Rs 12,000. That Rs 12,000, divided over 30 days, is Rs 400 a day, and Rs 12,000 — not Rs 60,000 — becomes the number in his head for the month. The shoes are now a thing he saves two months for, not a thing he can afford on the 2nd.
research.failure_mode: The allocation still breaks if Ali writes down only the bills that arrive as bills. His commitment list misses the things that are just as fixed but never invoiced — Rs 3,500 of petrol, a cousin's wedding gift, the annual bike insurance that lands in one month. He does the subtraction, gets a comfortable-looking Rs 12,000, spends against it honestly, and is still short on the 26th — now confused, because he "did the method." The allocation is only as true as the commitment list; anything predictable that is left off it simply gets paid out of the spending money without warning.
research.payoff: By the 24th of October, Ali knows before he opens his banking app roughly what the balance will say, because he decided it on the 1st. He has Rs 5,000 he did not have before, he has not borrowed from a friend, and when someone asks him on the 8th whether he can go in on a weekend trip, he can answer from the Rs 12,000 figure instead of guessing and finding out on the 18th.
misconceptions: "I'm broke because I don't earn enough" — for most months it is order of spending, not size of income; the same salary lasts when commitments come out first.
"I'll save whatever is left at the end of the month" — nothing is ever left; savings only happens as a slice taken on payday.
"I know my bills by heart, I don't need to write them down" — the recalled list is reliably smaller than the real one, and the gap is exactly what makes you short.
"The balance in my account is my money" — most of it is already promised to commitments that just haven't been debited yet.
"Allocating means I can never enjoy anything" — it means the enjoyment is funded from a known Rs 12,000 rather than borrowed from the rent.

quiz.stem: Ali earns Rs 60,000. His written commitments total Rs 43,000 and he moves Rs 5,000 to savings on payday. On the 2nd a friend asks him to join a weekend trip costing Rs 6,000. What should Ali check it against?
options: The Rs 55,000 still sitting in his account on the 2nd
The Rs 12,000 of spending money left after commitments and savings
His Rs 60,000 salary, since the trip is well under it
The Rs 5,000 in savings, which he can top up next month
quiz.explain: On the 2nd the account still looks full only because rent, the bike and the bills have not been debited yet — that money is already promised, so judging the trip against the balance is exactly the mistake that left Ali short in September. The only honest figure is what is left after commitments and savings come out: Rs 12,000, and a Rs 6,000 trip takes half of it.

reasons: One protagonist, Ali, in one running scenario (his September salary and then his October salary) followed in depth — no list of separate domain examples.
Exactly one concept: subtract what is already committed before deciding what is spendable.
Arc runs in order — friction (01–06), diagnosis and fix (07–14), structure (09–14), failure mode (16–19), payoff (20).

Beat 15 is a correctly formed checkpoint: no vo, no art, no info, sits between two spoken beats at 75% through, with a defensible answer the video has earned, three tempting distractors, and an explain written for the learner who chose the account balance.
20 beats, inside the 16–22 house range; every vo is one sentence that reads aloud naturally; no title cards.
Four different numeric data templates carry real numbers (bars 04, gauge 05, tally 10, bignum 12) and only one text-only card (17) — well clear of the text-slab gate.
Four motion beats (06, 09, 11, 16), all on story turns, all describing in-character movement only.
Every scene prompt describes a physical act (handing, taking, writing, dropping a coin, adding lines, lifting a jar) — none is a portrait; every ali beat has a single subject.
All art prompts specify flat 2D vector on plain cream, no ground/shadow/desk/dark fill, no letters/numbers/labels/signage, and Ali is described identically in all twelve.
Arithmetic is internally consistent: 22+6+7+3+5 = 43, 60 − 43 − 5 = 12, and 12,000 over 30 days ≈ 400 a day.
No blocking fixes remain. The minor items below are improvements only — the video works without them.

fixes.problem: The quiz object carries stem, options, answer and explain but no `correctNote`, which CLAUDE.md lists as part of the settled checkpoint shape enforced by qa-checkpoint.js. I cannot verify from the text provided whether that field is optional.
fixes.suggested: Add a one-line `correctNote` for the learner who chose right, e.g. "Exactly — the balance on the 2nd is mostly other people's money; Rs 12,000 is the only figure that is really his to spend." Confirm against qa-checkpoint.js before render.

fixes.problem: `tpl: "twocard"` is not one of the templates named in the house set (gauge, bignum, tally, bars, scoresheet, piles, statement). If it is not registered it would render blank; this cannot be confirmed from the script text alone.
fixes.suggested: Verify `twocard` exists in the info-card templates. If it does not, fall back to a `statement`-style two-column card or split the eight items into a `tally` with counts, keeping the text-card total at two or fewer.

fixes.problem: The tally row for rent carries count 22 and the rows total 43 marks; a tally template that draws one mark per unit could crowd or overflow at that scale.
fixes.suggested: Confirm the tally template groups marks in fives and wraps, or switch this beat to `bars` with the same five labels and values so 22 is a bar length rather than 22 glyphs.

fixes.problem: The named September spending (9,000 shoes + 4,000 lent + 22,000 rent + 7,000 bike = 42,000) does not by itself bring 60,000 down to the 2,000 shown on beat 05 — eating out four times would have to cost about 16,000.
fixes.suggested: Either add a catch-all to the sentence — "...eats out four times, lends a friend four thousand, and lets groceries and petrol go untracked" — or raise the beat 05 gauge value to something the named spending supports.

fixes.problem: All five tally rows are toned "bad", so the card reads as uniformly alarming when it is really just a neutral inventory of ordinary commitments.
fixes.suggested: Tone rent, bills and the installment "mid" and leave only the largest "bad", or drop tone entirely so the card reads as a list rather than a warning.

fixes.problem: The closing sentence is the longest in the script and carries two clauses plus a date, which slightly blunts the payoff beat.
fixes.suggested: Tighten to "By the twenty-fourth, Ali already knows what his app will say — and the five thousand is still there." and keep the "24 October" overlay.

BLOCKER: the checkpoint is missing `correctNote`; the house format is {stem, options, answer, correctNote, explain} and qa-checkpoint.js fails the build without it.

research.topic: "Lesson one" (series: demo, notes: [course-x]) — the topic as typed does not name a subject; it names a position in a course ("course-x") whose contents were not provided. Treated as: what Lesson One of a course has to accomplish — the opening lesson of a course, built so the learner can do one small real thing by the end of it.
research.interpretation: You typed "Lesson one" with the note [course-x], which names a slot in a course rather than a subject, and nothing in your message says what course-x is about — so rather than invent a subject, this video teaches what Lesson One itself must do: open on the learner's real problem and end with one thing they can actually do; retype with the course subject if you wanted Lesson One *of* something specific.
research.slo: Given a course outline, the learner can rewrite its first lesson so it opens on a concrete learner problem and closes with one small task the learner completes unaided.
research.audience: People building or teaching a course for the first time — trainers, L&D designers, subject experts asked to 'do the onboarding module'. They know their subject cold and can make slides; they have never had to think about what the first lesson costs them if it goes wrong.
key_points: The topic as typed names a slot, not a subject — 'course-x' was not defined in the brief, so this lesson teaches the design of a first lesson, not the content of one.
Lesson One's job is not coverage; it is to get the learner to do one real thing before they close the tab.
The first lesson should open on the problem the learner already has, not on definitions, history, or the syllabus.
Scope Lesson One to a single task the learner can finish unaided in the lesson's runtime — one task, not a tour.
Everything the learner does not need for that one task moves to Lesson Two or later; 'they'll need it eventually' is not a reason to put it first.
A first lesson is testable: watch one learner finish it without help, and fix what they stumbled on.
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches a 6-week evening course on spreadsheets for small-shop owners at a community centre in Lahore. Eighteen people signed up. He has 40 minutes for Lesson One on a Tuesday night, and his slide deck is 22 slides: the history of spreadsheets, the parts of the ribbon, a labelled diagram of rows, columns and cells, the difference between relative and absolute references, and a list of the 30 functions the course will cover. His learners are shopkeepers who came because they are tired of totalling the day's sales in a paper register at 10pm.
research.friction: Ali runs all 22 slides. At minute 34 he asks the class to open Excel and the room goes quiet — one man has not found the app, two have opened Word, and Zubaida asks a question about the ribbon diagram from slide 9 that reveals she has no idea what any of it was for. Nobody has typed a number into a cell. He ends the night having 'covered' cells, references and the function list, and hands out no task because there is no time. The next Tuesday, 11 of 18 come back; two tell him at the door that it seemed like it was going to be a lot of theory.
research.fix: Ali rebuilds Lesson One around one thing a shopkeeper can do that night: add up one day's sales in a spreadsheet. He cuts the deck to 3 slides. Minute 0 he does not define a spreadsheet — he holds up a paper register and asks who totalled theirs last night and how long it took. Minute 4 everyone has the app open and one column of their own real sales numbers typed in. Minute 12 they type =SUM of that column and watch the total appear. Minutes 12–35 they each do it again with a second day's figures, unaided, while Ali walks the room. History, the ribbon tour, relative vs absolute references and the 30-function list all move to later lessons — absolute references are not needed to total a column, so they are not in Lesson One.
research.failure_mode: Ali over-corrects the following term and makes Lesson One so small it teaches nothing that lasts: the class types numbers, presses =SUM, sees the total, and leaves without ever having entered their own data or repeated the task alone. It feels like a great session — everyone succeeded — but it was Ali's numbers on Ali's file, done once, with him narrating each click. Week 2, nobody can start a sheet from a blank screen. 'One small task' means one task the learner finishes unaided with their own material, not one demo they watched go by.
research.payoff: Ali's learners walk out of the first night with a working file on their own phone or laptop holding their own shop's takings, and a total that matches the register. He can now open Lesson Two on something they have already done instead of re-teaching from zero, and when he designs any later course he starts by naming the one task Lesson One must end with — then cuts everything that does not serve it.
misconceptions: That Lesson One should preview the whole course so learners know what is coming — a syllabus tour costs the minutes the first real task needs, and learners cannot hold a map of a place they have never been.
That foundations must come first, so definitions and vocabulary belong in the opening lesson — terms stick once the learner has done the thing the term names.
That a first lesson has failed if it covers less material than the others; Lesson One is measured by what the learner can do at the end, not by how much was said.
That Lesson One being 'the easy one' means it needs less design — it decides who comes back for Lesson Two, so it is the most designed lesson in the course.

quiz.stem: Ali is designing Lesson One of a new course. Which choice best fits what a first lesson is for?
options: Walk through the syllabus so learners know the whole course map before starting
Have learners complete one small real task with their own material, unaided
Teach the core definitions and vocabulary so later lessons have a foundation
Cover as much ground as the other lessons so week one isn't wasted
quiz.explain: A syllabus tour or a round of definitions feels responsible, but it spends the minutes the first real task needs, and terms stick after someone has done the thing the term names, not before. Week one is the only lesson whose job is to get a finished task out of every learner.

Nine of ten scenes describe a physical act.

BLOCKER: both `ali` beats (02, 06) show Ali holding a prop. The cutout segments the hero on `ali` beats, so a fan of cards held across the body and a stack held at his side get sliced or dropped — the recurring 'half-cut prop' defect that qa-cutouts.js hard-fails before art is bought. Both prompts even say 'props detached and floating' while describing him gripping them, which is the contradiction that produces the slice.
Remaining items are minor and do not hold the video back once the two mode changes are made.
